prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and timely topic: understanding what drives zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models. The central contribution is a structured review of prior work organized into five factor categories—linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data—with an explicit attempt to reconcile contradictory findings across studies. The topic is highly relevant to multilingual NLP, especially given the practical importance of transfer to low-resource languages and the persistent lack of consensus on why multilingual models transfer at all. Overall, I found the paper useful, reasonably well organized, and potentially valuable as a reference point for researchers entering the area. At the same time, as a review paper aiming to establish a “common understanding,” it falls short in methodological rigor and in the precision with which it synthesizes evidence. My overall assessment is positive but mixed: the paper has clear value, but it would benefit substantially from a more systematic review methodology, sharper distinctions between evidence and conjecture, and a more careful treatment of confounds and scope.

The strongest aspect of the paper is its framing. The five-way categorization is intuitive and covers much of the literature that practitioners would naturally consult when thinking about cross-lingual transfer. The paper also does more than merely list studies: in several places it tries to explain why findings differ, for example by distinguishing synthetic versus natural language experiments, structured versus random word-order perturbations, and linear versus nonlinear meta-models for transfer prediction. This effort to reconcile contradictions is commendable and more ambitious than many survey papers. I also appreciated the repeated emphasis that factors do not operate independently and that task type matters. Those are important messages that are often lost in simplified narratives such as “typological similarity helps” or “shared vocabulary is enough.”

The section on linguistic similarity is one of the more useful parts of the paper. The authors identify syntax/word order as the most frequently studied factor and correctly note that the literature is not as uniform as it may first appear. Their observation that random permutation or reversal may overstate the importance of syntax relative to naturally occurring typological variation is insightful and, if stated carefully, could be one of the paper’s more memorable takeaways. Likewise, the discussion of genetic, geographic, and phonological similarity usefully highlights that “linguistic similarity” is not a single construct. The table summarizing studies, tasks, models, language types, and metrics is also helpful.

That said, the review often moves too quickly from reported correlations to causal language. For example, statements such as certain features “contribute to” or “enable” transfer are stronger than what many cited studies actually establish. Much of the literature summarized here is observational, often based on correlations between transfer scores and language-distance features, or on synthetic interventions whose ecological validity is limited. The paper does acknowledge this in places, but not consistently enough. A review paper of this kind should be especially disciplined about distinguishing causal evidence from correlational evidence, and direct intervention studies from post hoc predictive analyses. Without that distinction, the synthesis risks overstating consensus.

A related concern is that the paper does not sufficiently separate three different scientific questions: what predicts transfer performance, what causes transfer performance, and what mechanistically explains internal cross-lingual alignment. These are not the same. A feature may be a good predictor of transfer language choice without being a mechanistic driver of multilingual representation alignment. Conversely, an architectural intervention may affect alignment without being the dominant predictor across natural language pairs. The paper sometimes blends these levels of analysis together. A stronger version would explicitly structure the review around evidence types: predictive meta-modeling, controlled synthetic interventions, natural-language comparative studies, and representation-level probing. That would make the “common understanding” more defensible.

The lexical overlap section is interesting and probably the most nuanced part of the paper, especially in its argument that lexical overlap matters more when word order differs or when source-language pre-training data is limited. This is a plausible and useful synthesis. However, the paper occasionally overreaches in claiming to “explain” prior contradictions. In several cases, the proposed explanations are hypotheses rather than demonstrated resolutions. For instance, the discussion of why Pires et al. and Tran and Bisazza differ from Wu and Dredze is suggestive, but the evidence presented in the review is indirect. Similarly, the explanation based on tree-based models versus Lasso regression in transfer prediction is plausible, but it remains speculative unless the review can point to direct comparative evidence. These hypotheses should be labeled more clearly as interpretations rather than settled conclusions.

The model architecture section is informative but comparatively thin. It focuses mainly on parameter sharing, depth, attention heads, and overparameterization. These are relevant, but the section feels narrower than the title suggests. For a review paper aspiring to broad coverage, I would expect more discussion of tokenizer-model interactions, encoder-only versus encoder-decoder architectures, multilingual versus bilingual scaling regimes, sparse or modular architectures, and perhaps the role of embedding space geometry or layerwise specialization. Even if the literature is sparse, the review should make that explicit and delineate what is known versus underexplored. As written, the section reads more like a summary of a few influential papers than a comprehensive synthesis of architectural factors.

The pre-training settings and pre-training data sections are useful but again somewhat uneven in rigor. The discussion of NSP, sequence length, vocabulary size, and tokenizer quality is relevant, and the paper correctly notes that tokenizer quality may matter more for token-level tasks. The pre-training data section also highlights an important point: target-language corpus size and corpus comparability matter, and their effects may vary by task. However, these sections would benefit from a more explicit treatment of confounding variables. For example, corpus size, domain, script, tokenizer quality, and language coverage are often entangled in multilingual pre-training setups. A review that aims to unify findings should repeatedly foreground these confounds rather than summarize results factor by factor as if they were cleanly separable. In practice, many reported effects may be partially mediated by other variables.

One notable weakness is the absence of a systematic review methodology. The paper mentions a list of surveyed papers in the appendix, but it does not clearly describe search strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, time window, venues searched, or how studies were categorized. For a narrative survey this may be acceptable at a minimal level, but the paper’s claims about consensus and conflict resolution would be much stronger if backed by a transparent methodology. As it stands, the reader cannot easily assess whether the literature coverage is comprehensive, whether there is selection bias toward certain tasks or model families, or whether contradictory evidence may have been omitted. The limitations section acknowledges selection bias and methodological heterogeneity, which is good, but these are not minor caveats here—they directly affect the credibility of the paper’s central synthesis.

The scope of the review is also narrower than the title suggests in one important respect. The title refers broadly to “multilingual language models,” but the actual discussion is dominated by encoder-style masked language models such as mBERT and XLM-R, with some bilingual BERT/RoBERTa variants and a few controlled studies. The paper briefly mentions generative models only in future work. Given the current landscape, this is understandable, but then the scope should be stated more explicitly up front. Otherwise, readers may infer that the conclusions generalize to multilingual seq2seq models, instruction-tuned LLMs, or decoder-only multilingual models, which is not established by the reviewed evidence.

I also found the treatment of “cultural context” underdeveloped relative to the framing in the abstract and introduction. The paper mentions cultural context several times as a factor worth considering, but it is not one of the five main categories, nor is there a dedicated section that systematically reviews evidence about it. As a result, the repeated references to cultural context feel somewhat disconnected from the actual structure of the paper. If the authors believe cultural context is a meaningful contributor to transfer performance, it deserves either its own section or a clearer explanation of how it interacts with the five chosen categories. Otherwise, it would be better to tone down its prominence in the framing.

There are also some issues of precision and presentation. The paper occasionally uses broad phrases such as “it has been shown” or “confirmed” where the underlying evidence is more mixed. Some conclusions are stronger than warranted by the cited studies. There are minor writing issues as well, including occasional redundancy, awkward phrasing, and a few typographical problems. These do not fundamentally undermine the paper, but they do matter for a review article whose main contribution is clarity of synthesis. The tables are helpful, but additional summary tables would improve usability—for example, a matrix of factors by task type, indicating whether evidence is strong, mixed, weak, or absent; or a table distinguishing evidence from natural-language studies versus synthetic interventions.

A major opportunity for improvement is to make the synthesis more analytical and less sequential. Right now, much of the paper proceeds factor by factor and study by study. A stronger review would culminate in a clearer integrative framework. For example, the authors could propose a hierarchy of evidence: lexical overlap and script sharing may primarily facilitate token-level anchoring; syntax may matter more when lexical cues are weak; pre-training data size and domain may dominate for higher-level semantic tasks; architecture and parameter sharing may modulate whether the model is forced into shared representations. Even if such a framework remains partly conjectural, articulating it explicitly would make the paper more than a catalog of findings. The current discussion section gestures in this direction but remains fairly high level.

I would also encourage the authors to be more explicit about evaluation artifacts. Cross-lingual transfer results are often benchmark-dependent, and many tasks differ not only in linguistic demands but also in annotation conventions, label semantics, translation artifacts, and domain mismatch. Some of the apparent task-specific effects summarized in the paper may partly reflect dataset construction rather than intrinsic differences between “syntactic” and “semantic” tasks. A review paper should at least flag this possibility. Similarly, the distinction between zero-shot transfer and translation-based transfer is introduced early, but the review could better explain how excluding translation-based settings affects the generality of its conclusions.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. It addresses a real need in the field, gathers a substantial body of literature, and offers several useful synthesis points. For readers seeking an entry point into the literature on cross-lingual transfer factors in multilingual encoders, this paper would likely be helpful. Its value is strongest as an organized narrative overview and weaker as a definitive resolution of the literature. If the authors revise it to be more systematic, more careful about causal claims, and more explicit about scope and evidence types, it could become a strong reference piece.

My recommendation would therefore be borderline positive, contingent on revision quality. The paper is relevant and potentially useful, but it needs stronger methodological grounding and sharper synthesis to fully support its ambitious title and claims.

The most important changes I would request are the following. First, add a transparent review methodology: search sources, keywords, date range, inclusion criteria, and categorization procedure. Second, clearly distinguish correlational findings, controlled interventions, and mechanistic probing, and avoid causal wording where not justified. Third, either add a dedicated treatment of cultural context or reduce its prominence in the framing. Fourth, sharpen the scope to clarify that the review primarily concerns encoder-style multilingual PLMs rather than multilingual language models in the broad contemporary sense. Fifth, provide a more integrative summary that maps factors to tasks, evidence strength, and likely interactions. Sixth, more clearly label speculative explanations for contradictory findings as hypotheses rather than resolutions.

In summary, this is a useful and timely review with a sensible taxonomy and several thoughtful synthesis attempts, but it currently lacks the methodological rigor and evidential precision needed to fully substantiate its claims of consensus-building and conflict resolution. With revision, it could become a valuable survey for the multilingual NLP community.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper is a narrative review of factors believed to influence zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models. It organizes prior work into five categories: linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data. The paper aims to synthesize empirical findings, identify areas of consensus, and explain contradictions across studies. It also discusses task-specific effects, interactions among factors, and future directions such as broader multilingual evaluation and extending analysis to generative models.
strengths: Timely and relevant topic: understanding cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models is important for both theory and practice.
Clear high-level taxonomy of factors affecting transfer, which helps structure a fragmented literature.
Broad coverage of prior work across multiple dimensions including linguistic, architectural, and data-related factors.
Useful effort to reconcile contradictory findings rather than merely listing papers.
Includes explicit discussion of limitations such as selection bias, publication bias, and heterogeneity of methodologies.
Highlights interaction effects and task dependence, which are often overlooked in simpler surveys.
weaknesses: The review is largely narrative and lacks a systematic survey methodology (e.g., search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality assessment), which weakens reproducibility and claims of comprehensiveness.
Several conclusions are speculative and not rigorously supported by the surveyed evidence; the paper often proposes explanations for contradictions without validating them.
The treatment of evidence is uneven: some sections are detailed while others are relatively shallow, especially for model architecture and pre-training settings.
No quantitative synthesis is provided (e.g., meta-analysis, standardized comparison tables beyond one subsection), making it difficult to assess strength of evidence across factors.
The paper sometimes overstates causal interpretations from correlational studies and feature-importance analyses.
The scope is somewhat diffuse: cultural context is mentioned repeatedly in the abstract/introduction, but it is not developed as a dedicated factor in the main taxonomy.
Writing quality is generally understandable but contains some imprecision, redundancy, and occasional grammatical issues.
methodological_flaws: The paper presents itself as a review but does not specify a systematic literature collection protocol. Without search databases, keywords, time span, screening procedure, or inter-reviewer agreement, the survey cannot be audited for completeness or bias.

A central scientific-logic issue is the frequent use of post hoc explanations to reconcile conflicting studies. For example, contradictions about lexical overlap and syntax are explained via hypothesized interactions, model class differences, or dataset properties, but these explanations are not independently substantiated within the review.

The paper sometimes treats feature importance from predictive meta-models (e.g., tree models, Lasso) as evidence about underlying causal factors. This is methodologically weak because feature importance is model-dependent, sensitive to collinearity, and not directly comparable across studies using different predictors and learning algorithms.

Some claims rely on synthetic-language experiments and are then generalized to natural-language transfer without sufficient caution. Although the discussion acknowledges this limitation, the main conclusions still occasionally extrapolate beyond what the evidence justifies.
The review claims to 'resolve conflicts among contradictory studies,' but in most cases it offers plausible interpretations rather than actual resolution supported by controlled comparative evidence.

There is an inconsistency in scope: cultural context is advertised as a key factor in the abstract and introduction, yet it is not operationalized as one of the five main categories nor systematically reviewed. This weakens conceptual coherence.

Empirical validity of cross-study comparisons is limited because tasks, language sets, metrics, models, and evaluation protocols differ substantially across cited works; the review notes this but still draws relatively strong cross-paper conclusions without normalization or formal evidence weighting.
